findings.claim: Architecture-contract check, decision by decision: sol-skill conflicts with Decision 3 and invariant 7, needs relocation to satisfy invariant 8, and falls outside the taxonomy of Decisions 1/2/5 rather than violating them. Decision 1 (five governors) is untouched — sol is a user-invoked workflow command, not a governor, and does not merge or split any governor. Decision 2's corollary ('no repo-specific fact may live in a governor's procedure') does not bind sol because it is not a governor — but sol's procedure is saturated with vendor-specific facts, which is exactly the class Decision 2 quarantines. Decision 3 is a direct conflict: the contract says 'every skill carries a NOT clause' and 'Every description here states WHEN, quotes situations, and names where near-miss cases go' — sol's 24-word description does none of the three, and its `disable-model-invocation: true` / `user-invocable: true` frontmatter creates a skill class the contract has no exemption for. Decision 4 (anti-ceremony valve) is formally missing from sol but functionally satisfied by manual-only invocation (README: 'Delegating to a second paid model is your call, not a decision Claude makes on your behalf mid-task'). Invariants 1, 2, 4 are actively REINFORCED by sol, not broken: evidence-strict ('never trust it as verification', 'Re-run the project's test/lint/typecheck commands yourself'), pre-commitment ordering (acceptance criteria written into the brief before implementation, 'each criterion phrased as a checkable command'), and flag-don't-fix ('<action_safety> — no unrelated changes, no drive-by refactors'). Invariant 7 is the clearest breakage: sol hardcodes the model id `gpt-5.6-sol`, effort `xhigh`, and (in README) 'Codex CLI ≥ 0.144' — all volatile facts, all undated, in a library whose invariant reads 'volatile facts carry dates' with breaking-it example 'Undated ... anywhere in the library'. Invariant 8 requires moving the file: sol ships at `skills/sol/SKILL.md`; the library's placement law is `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` — 'Any other layout — it fails silently'; the name `sol` already equals the directory basename, so only relocation is needed, no rename.

findings.claim: House-style adaptations required by skill-authoring — confirmed mechanically: the library's own lint script FAILS sol as-is. Running `lint_skill.sh` against the sol directory (2026-08-03) produced: 'FAIL: description has no trigger language', 'WARN: no Provenance section heading', 'WARN: no When NOT to use section heading', '== RESULT: FAIL =='. Adoption therefore requires at minimum: (a) rewriting the description to the three-job trigger contract (WHEN situation + quoted phrasings + NOT clause) — note sol currently keeps its routing logic in the BODY ('do NOT invoke Sol, unless the user explicitly names Sol as the researcher ("sol research…", "have sol research", "ask sol")'), which the house mistakes list names as 'Trigger logic in the body (dead text)'; for a user-invoked skill the body does load on invocation, but the lint still fails the description; (b) date-stamping the volatile facts with the three confidence labels (verified/assumption/candidate): model id gpt-5.6-sol, codex ≥ 0.144, the 10-minute timeout, the 8m02s benchmark — all currently undated; (c) adding the two missing house sections, 'When NOT to use this skill' (naming siblings — e.g. plain research routes to the planner, high-risk review overlap with adversarial-verify) and a final 'Provenance and maintenance' with re-verify one-liners (obvious candidates: `codex --version`, `bash scripts/check-codex.sh` — sol already ships the re-verify tooling, it just isn't framed as a Provenance section); (d) checklist friction: step 5's '≥3 should-fire prompts and ≥2 should-not-fire near-misses' and step 7's live-fire trigger test are ill-defined for a skill that never auto-fires — the library would need a command-skill variant of the checklist; (e) sol's extra frontmatter fields (version, argument-hint, disable-model-invocation, user-invocable, allowed-tools, homepage, repository, author, license) parse cleanly under the lint but are undocumented in domain-reference, whose model is 'YAML frontmatter (name, description)' — skill-authoring's own maintenance rule says new frontmatter fields go 'via domain-reference first'; (f) minor: the naming rule 'says what the skill is FOR, not how it works' cuts against the name `sol` (names the vendor model, not the function), though renaming would break the upstream /sol muscle memory.

findings.claim: Install-footprint (Decision 5 / domain-reference consequence 2): sol's per-session context cost is small in absolute terms — its description measures 24 words (lint output), versus the library's '~130 words each' mean — so a personal install costs at most a 24-word description line in every session on the machine, and a per-project install confines that to repos where codex is actually set up. But under the library's own doctrine the cost-benefit is anomalous in both directions: (a) because `disable-model-invocation: true` means the skill 'fires only when you type it' (README), the description buys ZERO auto-routing value, and skill-authoring's rule is 'every installed description is permanent context, so each word must earn its routing value' — a description that can never route earns nothing per that ledger, making sol either exempt (if the platform drops user-only skills from the always-in-context roster — unverified here, and domain-reference's mental model has no category for disable-model-invocation skills at all) or pure-cost-but-tiny; (b) Decision 5's binary — governors installed personally because they 'govern all work and earn that cost', support skills per-project because they 'matter only when working ON the library' — has no slot for a manual tool skill whose usefulness is gated not by which repo you're in but by per-MACHINE state (Codex CLI ≥ 0.144 + `codex login` + a ChatGPT plan), which domain-reference's own corollary flags: 'Capabilities are equally per-surface'. Net: personal install on codex-equipped machines is the natural fit and the context price is ~1/5 of one governor description, but slotting it is an owner call of the same class as assumption A3 ('owner-adjustable, not doctrine'), and adopting it forces domain-reference to document the disable-model-invocation class before Decision 5's cost math can even be applied to it.

findings.claim: Precedence law (Decision 2): the law as written does not bind sol at all — it governs 'a project that carries its own instance of a law' versus 'the governor', and sol is neither a governor nor a law with project instances, so no defined precedence relation applies. The real interaction is inverse and currently unregulated: sol's brief contract embeds its own miniature instances of three governors' laws — '<non_goals> — explicit scope fence' and '<action_safety> — no unrelated changes, no drive-by refactors' mirror scope-fence/invariant 4; 'never trust it as verification' plus 'Re-run the project's test/lint/typecheck commands yourself' mirror adversarial-verify/invariant 1; checkable acceptance criteria written before implementation mirror invariant 2's pre-commitment ordering. These are ALIGNED duplications, so when a personally-installed governor fires during a /sol run the result is a double-load of compatible law — the same 'acceptable cost' overlap class as weak-point 2, not a contradiction. The one genuine gap adoption would surface: the library has no written rule for precedence between an INVOKED command skill's procedure and a TRIGGERED governor — e.g. sol's hard rule 'Claude never edits production code in this flow' versus any governor-era inclination for Claude to apply a fix directly; sol resolves that internally (corrections route back through 'codex exec resume --last' as a file:line delta, capped at 2 rounds), but Decision 2 would need an extension — or an explicit statement of non-applicability — to cover the command-skill-vs-governor case, since today 'project instance wins over governor' is the library's only conflict-resolution law and it is silent here.

analysis.summary: Adopting sol-skill into claude-core-skills is feasible but it enters as a new, un-taxonomized species — a user-invoked, never-auto-firing command skill in a library whose entire doctrine (description-as-trigger, context-cost math, governor-vs-instance precedence) assumes model-invoked skills. What it takes: relocate to .claude/skills/sol/SKILL.md (invariant 8; the name already matches), rewrite the 24-word description to the three-job contract since the library's own lint FAILS it today ('description has no trigger language') plus WARNs on both missing house sections, add When-NOT and Provenance sections, and date-stamp the undated volatile facts (gpt-5.6-sol, codex ≥ 0.144, xhigh/10-min timeout) per invariant 7 — the clearest hard breach. What it breaks: nothing in the governors' substance — sol's brief contract independently re-implements invariants 1, 2, and 4 (evidence-strict review, pre-committed checkable criteria, no drive-by refactors), so co-firing governors double-load aligned law (weak-point-2-class cost, not contradiction). The precedence law does not touch sol (it is neither governor nor instance), exposing a gap: the library has no rule for invoked-command-vs-triggered-governor conflicts such as sol's 'Claude never edits production code'. Footprint-wise, personal install costs at most a 24-word description (~1/5 of one governor) that buys zero routing value since the skill only fires when typed, and its real gating is per-machine (codex CLI + ChatGPT plan), so the Decision 5 slotting is an A3-class owner call that first requires domain-reference to document the disable-model-invocation frontmatter class.

Overlooked within scope, none conclusion-flipping: (1) Cost-math interaction between Claims 2 and 3 — the required three-job description rewrite (Claim 2a) would grow sol's description from 24 words toward the library's 100–165-word class (skill-authoring Axis 2: 'This library's descriptions measure 100–165 words (mean ~128, 2026-07-11)', hard cap ≤1000 chars per the 1024-char platform limit), so Claim 3's '24-word / ~1/5 of a governor' footprint describes the pre-adoption artifact only; post-adoption cost is roughly a full governor-class description. The analysis never reconciles this. (2) Claim 1 announces a decision-by-decision walk but skips Decisions 6 and 7: Decision 6 ('Every governor ends with a Provenance section') is only functionally covered via Claim 2(c), and Decision 7's retirement evidence (base-model behavior already supplying a skill's value drove live-state-truth's retirement) is the library's own precedent for demanding measured behavioral delta before adopting any new always-installed skill — directly relevant to slotting sol, unmentioned. (3) Checklist step 8 unaddressed: 'behavioral edits to an existing skill go through research-methodology' and 'update the README inventory' — adoption trips both; also step 6's 'The script does NOT check the NOT clause; verify that by eye' means lint PASS alone would not close Claim 2(a). (4) Prior art uncited: /home/user/claude-core-skills/results/2026-07-13/external-skill-analysis/ (REPORT.md + analysis-result.json) is an existing library exercise evaluating an external skill against this same contract, including the finding that lint_skill.sh ignores allowed-tools/disable-model-invocation fields and that trigger collision with an existing skill's quoted phrasings is 'trust erosion' under Decision 3 — a template and precedent the synthesis step should know exists. (5) Minor: sol's `allowed-tools: Bash, Read, Write, Grep, Glob` includes Write despite 'Claude never edits production code' — consistent (scratchpad briefs need Write) but worth one line in any adoption review.
